claim: There has been debate about whether addition of an irrelevant distractor option to an otherwise binary decision influences which of the two choices is taken.
source: There has been debate about whether addition of an irrelevant distractor option to an otherwise binary decision influences which of the two choices is taken.
evidence: This is a statement about the existence of scientific debate, which is established through the literature cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Disparate views on whether distractors influence decisions are reconciled if distractors exert two opposing but not mutually exclusive effects.
source: We show that disparate views on this question are reconciled if distractors exert two opposing but not mutually exclusive effects.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: A positive distractor effect predicts high-value distractors improve decision-making.
source: Each effect predominates in a different part of decision space: (1) a positive distractor effect predicts high-value distractors improve decision-making
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that is tested and supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A negative distractor effect, of the type associated with divisive normalisation models, entails decreased accuracy with increased distractor values.
source: (2) a negative distractor effect, of the type associated with divisive normalisation models, entails decreased accuracy with increased distractor values.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction based on divisive normalization models that is tested in the manuscript.

claim: Both positive and negative distractor effects coexist in human decision making but in different parts of a decision space defined by the choice values.
source: Here, we demonstrate both distractor effects coexist in human decision making but in different parts of a decision space defined by the choice values.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by behavioral data analysis.

claim: Disruption of the medial intraparietal area (MIP) by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) increases positive distractor effects at the expense of negative distractor effects.
source: We show disruption of the medial intraparietal area (MIP) by transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) increases positive distractor effects at the expense of negative distractor effects.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by TMS intervention and behavioral data.

claim: Individuals with larger MIP volumes are less susceptible to the disruption induced by TMS.
source: Furthermore, individuals with larger MIP volumes are also less susceptible to the disruption induced by TMS.
evidence: This is supported by voxel-based morphometry analysis showing correlation between MIP volume and TMS effects.

claim: There is a causal link between MIP and the impact of distractors on decision-making via divisive normalisation.
source: These findings also demonstrate a causal link between MIP and the impact of distractors on decision-making via divisive normalisation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the TMS intervention effects on behavior.

claim: Binary choices have been studied extensively.
source: While binary choices have been studied extensively, there has been growing interest in complex decisions with more response alternatives (Albantakis et al., 2012; Chung et al., 2017; Churchland et al., 2008; Kohl et al., 2019; Churchland and Ditterich, 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, supported by citations.

claim: There has been growing interest in complex decisions with more response alternatives.
source: While binary choices have been studied extensively, there has been growing interest in complex decisions with more response alternatives (Albantakis et al., 2012; Chung et al., 2017; Churchland et al., 2008; Kohl et al., 2019; Churchland and Ditterich, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations indicating research trends.

claim: Introducing seemingly irrelevant 'distractor' alternatives influences decisions between the options of interest.
source: It has been claimed that introducing seemingly irrelevant 'distractor' alternatives influences decisions between the options of interest (Chung et al., 2017; Chau et al., 2014; Spektor et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Most evidence suggests that relative preferences between two options crucially depend on the value of added distractor options.
source: However, while most evidence suggests that relative preferences between two options crucially depend on the value of added distractor options (Chau et al., 2014; Louie et al., 2013; Louie et al., 2011), there is little consensus regarding the most fundamental feature of the nature of the distractor's influence – whether it makes decision-making worse or better – and the underlying neural mechanisms affecting these preferences.
evidence: This is a summary of the literature supported by citations.

claim: There is little consensus regarding whether distractors make decision-making worse or better.
source: However, while most evidence suggests that relative preferences between two options crucially depend on the value of added distractor options (Chau et al., 2014; Louie et al., 2013; Louie et al., 2011), there is little consensus regarding the most fundamental feature of the nature of the distractor's influence – whether it makes decision-making worse or better – and the underlying neural mechanisms affecting these preferences.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field based on the literature.

claim: Divisive normalisation is a potential mechanism underlying distractor effects.
source: One potential mechanism underlying this phenomenon is divisive normalisation.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on prior literature.

claim: Divisive normalisation is based on principles of normalisation observed in sensory systems.
source: Based on the principles of normalisation observed in sensory systems (Carandini and Heeger, 1994; Heeger, 1992), Louie and colleagues (Louie et al., 2011) proposed that the encoded value of a given stimulus corresponds to the stimulus' absolute value divided by the weighted sum of the absolute values of co-occurring stimuli.
evidence: This is a theoretical framework from the literature supported by citations.

claim: In divisive normalisation, the encoded value of a given stimulus corresponds to the stimulus' absolute value divided by the weighted sum of the absolute values of co-occurring stimuli.
source: Based on the principles of normalisation observed in sensory systems (Carandini and Heeger, 1994; Heeger, 1992), Louie and colleagues (Louie et al., 2011) proposed that the encoded value of a given stimulus corresponds to the stimulus' absolute value divided by the weighted sum of the absolute values of co-occurring stimuli.
evidence: This is a theoretical model from the literature.

claim: Divisive normalisation hypothesis suggests that neural responses during decision-making or accuracy in decision-making are increased as the value of the best option increases and as the values of the remaining alternatives decrease.
source: Despite differences in how exactly divisive normalisation is formalized (e.g. noise and weight assumptions), in general the hypothesis suggests that neural responses during decision-making or accuracy in decision-making are increased as the value of the best option increases and as the values of the remaining alternatives decrease.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction of the divisive normalization model.

claim: Divisive normalisation hypothesis receives empirical support in a number of studies in humans and monkeys.
source: This hypothesis receives empirical support in a number of studies in humans and monkeys (Louie et al., 2013; Khaw et al., 2017; Louie et al., 2014; Pastor-Bernier and Cisek, 2011; Rorie et al., 2010; Webb et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations from the literature.

claim: Divisive normalisation can be applicable to multi-attribute choices, as normalisation can occur at the level of individual attributes before they are combined into an overall option value.
source: Recently, there has been support for this view from experiments showing that divisive normalisation can be applicable to multi-attribute choices, as normalisation can occur at the level of individual attributes before they are combined into an overall option value (Landry and Webb, 2021; Dumbalska et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by recent experimental findings cited.

claim: Human participants displayed lower accuracy scores when a third low-value, rather than a third high-value option, was presented.
source: A seemingly opposing effect has been reported by Chau et al., 2014. They reported that human participants, who were asked to choose between two alternatives, displayed lower accuracy scores when a third low-value, rather than a third high-value option, was presented.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Chau and colleagues modelled their behavioural findings using a biophysically plausible mutual inhibition model, in which different choice alternatives are represented by competing neural populations.
source: Chau and colleagues modelled their behavioural findings using a biophysically plausible mutual inhibition model, in which different choice alternatives are represented by competing neural populations.
evidence: This is a description of a modeling approach from a cited study.

claim: In the mutual inhibition model, recurrent excitation within, and inhibition between populations create attractor dynamics, with one population displaying the highest firing rates, thereby indicating the choice of the associated response alternative.
source: Recurrent excitation within, and inhibition between populations create attractor dynamics, with one population displaying the highest firing rates, thereby indicating the choice of the associated response alternative (Wang, 2002).
evidence: This is a description of model dynamics supported by a citation.

claim: When a third option of high value, as opposed to low value, is added, inhibition between the populations is greater, which slows down the choice of the network such that it is less susceptible to noise and more capable of distinguishing between values.
source: When a third option of high value, as opposed to low value, is added, however, inhibition between the populations is greater. This slows down the choice of the network such that it is less susceptible to noise and more capable of distinguishing between values, particularly when the value difference between the two available options is small.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the mutual inhibition model.

claim: Blood oxygen-level dependent signals associated with a key decision variable, the value difference between the two available options, in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) were weaker when the distractor values were lower.
source: Chau et al., 2014 reported just such a change in behaviour and further explored the mechanisms mediating the effect using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). Blood oxygen-level dependent signals associated with a key decision variable, the value difference between the two available options, in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) were weaker when the distractor values were lower, further supporting the model predictions.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited fMRI study.

claim: Neural activity in the medial intraparietal area (MIP) of the parietal cortex showed patterns consistent with divisive normalisation.
source: Despite the fact that these findings appeared to stand in contrast to divisive normalisation, Chau and colleagues (Chau et al., 2014), also noted that neural activity in the medial intraparietal area (MIP) of the parietal cortex showed patterns consistent with divisive normalisation.
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: It has been argued that neither the negative distractor effects predicted by divisive normalisation models nor the positive distractor effects predicted by mutual inhibition models are robust.
source: Recently, however, it has been argued that neither the negative distractor effects predicted by divisive normalisation models nor the positive distractor effects predicted by mutual inhibition models are robust (Gluth et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Both positive and negative distractor effects occur but predominate to different degrees in different circumstances.
source: One way of reconciling these disparate points of view (positive distractor effects; negative distractor effects; no distractor effects), however, is the notion that, in fact, both positive and negative distractor effects occur but predominate to different degrees in different circumstances.
evidence: This is a theoretical reconciliation proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: A dual-route model that contains both a 'divisive normalisation' component and a 'mutual inhibition' component that run in parallel for making a decision in a race can reconcile disparate views on distractor effects.
source: This can be achieved by having a dual-route model that contains both a 'divisive normalisation' component and a 'mutual inhibition' component that run in parallel for making a decision in a race (Chau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a theoretical model from the literature.

claim: The negative influence of the distractor should be most prominent when the total sum of option values is low.
source: For example, careful consideration of the dual-route model suggests that the negative influence of the distractor should be most prominent in certain parts of a 'decision space' defined by two dimensions –the total sum and the difference in values of the options (Chau et al., 2020). Firstly, in the divisive normalisation component, the negative impact caused by variance in distractor value should be greatest when the total sum of option values is low.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the dual-route model.

claim: Distractors reliably exert a significant and negative effect on decision-making when the sum of the values of the choosable options is small.
source: In accordance with this prediction, distractors reliably exert a significant and negative effect on decision-making, when the sum of the values of the choosable options is small (Chau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an empirical finding from a cited study.

claim: Positive distractor effects should predominate when the values of both choosable options are close and decisions are difficult.
source: Secondly, positive distractor effects should predominate in the parts of the decision space in which the values of both choosable options are close and decisions are difficult but the opposite should happen when decisions are easy to make because the choice option values are far apart.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction tested in the study.

claim: Both positive and negative distractor effects are apparent even in data sets in which they have been claimed to be absent.
source: Both positive and negative distractor effects are apparent even in data sets in which they have been claimed to be absent (Chau et al., 2014; Chau et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about reanalysis of existing data supported by citations.

claim: If both types of distractor effect exist, then one might be promoted at the expense of the other by a manipulation that made decision-making relatively more dependent on different parts of the distributed neural circuit mediating decision-making.
source: Another prediction of this composite model is that if both types of distractor effect exist, then one might be promoted at the expense of the other by a manipulation that made decision-making relatively more dependent on different parts of the distributed neural circuit mediating decision-making.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction that motivates the TMS experiment.

claim: If the negative distractor effects linked to divisive normalisation are associated with intraparietal cortical areas such as MIP, then disrupting MIP should decrease their prevalence at the expense of the positive distractor effects associated with other decision-making areas such as vmPFC.
source: For example, if the negative distractor effects linked to divisive normalisation are associated with intraparietal cortical areas such as MIP, then disrupting MIP should decrease their prevalence at the expense of the positive distractor effects associated with other decision-making areas such as vmPFC.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the study.

claim: All participants displayed above chance performance in the main decision-making task with an average accuracy of 72.84%.
source: All participants displayed above chance performance in both the main decision-making task, and the "matching" trials (additional trials that aimed to prevent participants from ignoring the identity of the distractor; see Methods), with an average accuracy of 72.84% (SD = 6.71; Figure 2a)
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: All participants displayed above chance performance in the matching trials with an average accuracy of 70.14%.
source: All participants displayed above chance performance in both the main decision-making task, and the "matching" trials (additional trials that aimed to prevent participants from ignoring the identity of the distractor; see Methods), with an average accuracy of 72.84% (SD = 6.71; Figure 2a), and 70.14% (SD = 8.75) respectively
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The average RT of the main task was 887.71ms.
source: The average RT of the main task was 887.71ms (SD = 102.17ms; Figure 2b).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: There were no differences in accuracy between Non-TMS trials in MIP and MT sessions.
source: There were no differences in either accuracy, t(30) = 1.14, p=0.265, Cohen's d (d)=0.14, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [–0.01, 0.03], or reaction time (RT), t(30) = 0.64, p=0.525, d=0.11, CI = [–23.61, 45.33], between Non-TMS trials in MIP and MT sessions (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: There were no differences in reaction time between Non-TMS trials in MIP and MT sessions.
source: There were no differences in either accuracy, t(30) = 1.14, p=0.265, Cohen's d (d)=0.14, 95% confidence interval (CI) = [–0.01, 0.03], or reaction time (RT), t(30) = 0.64, p=0.525, d=0.11, CI = [–23.61, 45.33], between Non-TMS trials in MIP and MT sessions (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison of experimental conditions.

claim: There was a negative (HV-LV)(D–HV) effect on accuracy, suggesting that the distractor effect varied as a function of difficulty.
source: GLM1 revealed that there was a negative (HV-LV)(D–HV) effect on accuracy, suggesting that the distractor effect (i.e. D–HV) varied as a function of difficulty (i.e. HV-LV).
evidence: This is a finding from GLM analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: On Non-TMS trials, there was a positive HV-LV effect on accuracy.
source: On Non-TMS trials, there was a positive HV-LV effect (t(30) = 17.09, p<0.001, d=3.07, CI = [0.69, 0.88]; Figure 2c)
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM analysis.

claim: On Non-TMS trials, there was a negative HV +LV effect on accuracy, suggesting that more accurate choices were made on trials that consisted of options with poorer values.
source: On Non-TMS trials, there was a positive HV-LV effect (t(30) = 17.09, p<0.001, d=3.07, CI = [0.69, 0.88]; Figure 2c) and a negative HV +LV effect (t(30) = –4.35, p<0.001, d=–0.78, CI = [-0.38,–0.14]), suggesting that more accurate choices were made on trials that were easier and consisted of options with poorer values.
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM analysis with interpretation.

claim: There was no D-HV main effect on accuracy in Non-TMS trials.
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM analysis.

claim: There was a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) interaction effect on accuracy in Non-TMS trials.
source: but critically there was a negative (HV-LV)(D-HV) interaction effect (t(30) = –3.52, p=0.001, d=–0.63, CI = [-0.16,–0.04]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM analysis.

claim: On hard trials with small HV-LV, there was a positive D-HV effect on accuracy.
source: On hard trials with small HV-LV, there was a positive D-HV effect (t(30) = 2.62, p=0.014, d=0.47, CI = [0, 0.02]; Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM2 analysis shown in Figure 2d.

claim: On easy trials with large HV-LV, there was a negative D-HV effect on accuracy.
source: whereas on easy trials with large HV-LV, there was a negative D-HV effect (t(30) = –3.15, p=0.004, d=–0.57, CI = [–0.01, 0]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM2 analysis.

claim: Higher accuracy was associated with larger HV-LV differences in control Non-TMS data.
source: The results of GLM3 confirmed once again that in the control data, on average, higher accuracy was associated with larger HV-LV differences (t(30) = 17.04, p<0.001, d=3.06, CI = [0.76, 0.97]; Figure 3a)
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM3 analysis shown in Figure 3a.

claim: Higher accuracy was associated with lower HV +LV sum values in control Non-TMS data.
source: The results of GLM3 confirmed once again that in the control data, on average, higher accuracy was associated with larger HV-LV differences (t(30) = 17.04, p<0.001, d=3.06, CI = [0.76, 0.97]; Figure 3a) and lower HV +LV sum values (t(30) = –3.50, p=0.001, d=0.63, CI = [-0.33,–0.09]; Figure 3b).
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM3 analysis shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The average impact of D-HV on accuracy was not significant in control Non-TMS data.
source: The average impact of D-HV on accuracy was not significant (t(30) = 0.69, p=0.496, d=–0.12, CI = [–0.08, 0.16]; Figure 3c)
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM3 analysis shown in Figure 3c.

claim: The D-HV predictor showed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Site x Stimulation x Distractor Location) on accuracy.
source: Critically, however, the D-HV predictor showed a statistically significant three-way interaction (Site x Stimulation x Distractor Location: F(1,30) = 4.44, p=0.044, ηp2 p20.13; Figure 3c).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In the contralateral data set, there was a significant Site x Stimulation interaction effect on the D-HV predictor.
source: In the contralateral data, we found a significant Site x Stimulation interaction effect, F(1,26) = 4.99, p=0.034, ηp2p20.16 (no other effects were significant, F<0.73, p>0.400)
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on contralateral trials.

claim: There was a significant effect of TMS on MIP conditions on the D-HV predictor.
source: We found a significant effect of TMS on MIP conditions (F(1,24) = 4.32, p=0.049, ηp2p20.15), with TMS trials showing a more positive D-HV effect than Non-TMS trials.
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on MIP conditions.

claim: The MIP-TMS effect became even clearer after the grey matter volume (GM) of the same region was entered as a covariate.
source: The MIP-TMS effect became even clearer after the grey matter volume (GM) of the same region was also entered as a covariate (F(1,23) = 7.02, p=0.014, ηp2p20.23; the next section explains the importance of considering the GM and explains how the GM indices were obtained).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA with GM as covariate.

claim: There was no effect of TMS in MT conditions on the D-HV predictor.
source: In contrast, we found no effect in MT conditions (F(1,24) = 1.24, p=0.277, ηp2p20.05), and this lack of TMS effect was confirmed by an additional Bayesian test (BF10=0.225).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA and Bayesian analysis on MT conditions.

claim: The effect of MIP TMS on the distractor value's (D-HV) impact on decision accuracy showed a negative relationship with MIP GM.
source: Interestingly, the effect of MIP TMS on the distractor value's (D-HV) impact on decision accuracy showed a negative relationship with MIP GM (p=0.029, TFCE corrected, centred around MNI X(–30), Y(–52), Z(42), Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a result from VBM analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: In individuals with larger MIP GMs, there was less difference between TMS and Non-TMS trials because TMS had a weaker impact on disrupting the MIP-related negative distractor effect.
source: This implies that in individuals with larger MIP GMs, there was less difference between TMS and Non-TMS trials (less relative increase in the positive distractor effect at the expense of the negative distractor effect), because TMS had a weaker impact on disrupting the MIP-related negative distractor effect.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the VBM results.

claim: There was a significant partial correlation between MIP GM and MIP TMS impact on the D-HV effect.
source: First, we illustrate the VBM results again by showing that there was a significant partial correlation between MIP GM and MIP TMS impact on the D-HV effect (r(27) = –0.61, p<0.001; Figure 4b, left panel), after controlling for the other explanatory variables entered in the VBM (i.e. TMS effects on HV-LV and HV +LV).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: There was no correlation between MIP GM and TMS effect when it was estimated in the control sessions where MT was stimulated.
source: First, there was no correlation between MIP GM and TMS effect when it was estimated in the control sessions where MT was stimulated (r(27) = –0.05, p=0.816; Figure 4b right).
evidence: This is a statistical result from correlation analysis shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Larger D-HV values were related to more gaze shifts between D and HV.
source: First, we showed that larger D-HV values were related to more gaze shifts between D and HV (t(30) = 4.75, p<0.001, d=0.85, CI = [0.03, 0.08]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM3 analysis of eye-tracking data.

claim: There was a significant Site ×Stimulation interaction effect on the D-HV predictor for gaze shifts between HV and D.
source: The results showed a significant Site ×Stimulation interaction effect, F(1,25) = 8.85, p=0.006, ηp2p20.26.
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on eye-tracking data.

claim: In MIP sessions, the effect of distractor value on gaze shifts was significantly higher in TMS compared to Non-TMS trials.
source: Follow-up ANOVAs with factors of Side and Stimulation revealed in MIP sessions the effect of distractor value on gaze shifts was significantly higher in TMS compared to Non-TMS trials (F(1,25) = 5.30, p=0.030, ηp2p20.18)
evidence: This is a statistical result from follow-up ANOVA on eye-tracking data.

claim: In MT sessions, there was no significant difference in the effect of distractor value on gaze shifts between TMS and Non-TMS trials.
source: while in MT sessions there was no significant difference between TMS and Non-TMS trials (F(1,25) = 1.62, p=0.214, ηp2p20.06).
evidence: This is a statistical result from follow-up ANOVA on eye-tracking data.

claim: There was a significant two-way Site by Stimulation interaction effect on the D-HV predictor for gaze shifts between HV and D when collapsing across Side conditions.
source: Again, the results showed a significant two-way interaction effect, F(1,30) = 6.73, p=0.014, ηp2p20.18 (Figure 5a, right; Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on eye-tracking data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: A Site by Stimulation interaction was found for gaze shifts from D to HV.
source: When we performed a two-way ANOVA, a Site by Stimulation interaction was only found in the D-to-HV direction (F(1,30) = 5.82, p=0.022, ηp2p20.16; Figure 5b, right)
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on directional eye-tracking data shown in Figure 5b.

claim: No Site by Stimulation interaction was found for gaze shifts from HV to D.
source: but not the HV-to-D direction (F(1,30) = 1.03, p=0.319, ηp2p20.03; Figure 5c, right).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on directional eye-tracking data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Increased numbers of gaze shifts towards the low-value option were associated with lower accuracy.
source: We found that increased numbers of gaze shifts towards the low-value option were associated with lower accuracy (HV to LV: t(26) = –4.6, p<0.001, d=–0.88, CI = [-0.21,–0.08]; D to LV: t(26) = –4.74, p<0.001, d=–0.91, CI = [-0.19,–0.07]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM4 analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Increased accuracy was associated with increased gaze shifts from the distractor to the high-value option.
source: Importantly, we found increased accuracy to be associated with increased gaze shifts from the distractor to the high-value option (D to HV: t(26) = 5.77, p<0.001, d=1.11, CI = [0.13, 0.27]).
evidence: This is a statistical result from GLM4 analysis.

claim: The negative distractor effect predicted by divisive normalisation models is associated with intraparietal sulcal regions, such as MIP and LIP.
source: The negative distractor effect predicted by divisive normalisation models is associated with intraparietal sulcal regions, such as MIP and LIP (Chau et al., 2014; Louie et al., 2013; Louie et al., 2011)
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citations.

claim: The positive distractor effect has been linked with vmPFC.
source: while the positive distractor effect has been linked with vmPFC (Chau et al., 2014; Fouragnan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citations.

claim: After disrupting the parietal cortex using TMS, the negative distractor effect was reduced and the remaining positive distractor effect emerged more robustly.
source: In the current study, we demonstrated that after disrupting the parietal cortex using TMS, the negative distractor effect was reduced and so the remaining positive distractor effect emerged more robustly (Figures 3c and 6b).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study shown in Figures 3c and 6b.

claim: The MIP region in which grey matter variance predicted variance in the size of MIP TMS effects was slightly anterior to the MIP region targeted with TMS.
source: Notably, we found that the MIP region in which grey matter variance predicted variance in the size of MIP TMS effects was slightly anterior to the MIP region targeted with TMS.
evidence: This is an observation from the VBM analysis.

claim: A causal relation between the vmPFC and a positive distractor effect has been observed in both humans and monkeys.
source: In contrast, a causal relation between the vmPFC and a positive distractor effect has been observed in both humans and monkeys (Noonan et al., 2010; Noonan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a claim from the literature supported by citations.

claim: In both humans and monkeys, individuals with vmPFC lesions, unlike control or pre-operative individuals, were less accurate in their decisions when high-value distractors were presented.
source: In both species, individuals with vmPFC lesions, unlike control or pre-operative individuals, were less accurate in their decisions when high-value distractors were presented.
evidence: This is a finding from cited lesion studies.

claim: The positive distractor effect, which is linked to vmPFC, is mediated by overt attention.
source: It has been argued that the positive distractor effect, which is linked to vmPFC, is mediated by overt attention.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the literature.

claim: According to the mutual inhibition model, the presence of an appealing distractor can boost the overall inhibition in a neural network and avoid stochastic choices.
source: According to the mutual inhibition model, the presence of an appealing distractor can boost the overall inhibition in a neural network and avoid stochastic choices.
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from the mutual inhibition model.

claim: When people are allowed to revise their choice after a brief delay, they tend to make more accurate decisions afterwards.
source: These models suggest that the evidence accumulation process, which guides decision-making, continues even after an initial decision is made. When people are allowed to revise their choice after a brief delay, they tend to make more accurate decisions afterwards.
evidence: This is a finding from cited studies on changes of mind.

claim: Gaze shifts from the distractor to the high-value option were associated with increased accuracy.
source: In the current study, we found that these gaze shifts from the distractor to the high-value option were indeed associated with increased accuracy
evidence: This is a finding from the eye-tracking analysis.

claim: Gaze shifts from the distractor to the high-value option were promoted when the positive distractor effect became more prominent after MIP TMS.
source: and crucially, that these gaze shifts were promoted when the positive distractor effect became more prominent after MIP TMS (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is a finding from the eye-tracking analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: A positive distractor effect can be induced in some regions of distractor space in divisive normalisation-based models.
source: It is important to note that a positive distractor effect can be induced in some regions of distractor space in divisive normalisation-based models (Louie et al., 2013; Webb et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim from the literature supported by citations.
